title: Poland, 1939: five dates, different kinds of change
subtitle: An introduction to the first Ostfront Atlas timeline
author: R.G. Cruise
body:
The partition of Poland in 1939 was a sequence of decisions, invasions and imposed settlements. The familiar image of German and Soviet territory meeting along a dividing line shows an outcome, but it cannot explain how that outcome was produced. A secret agreement was not yet an occupation; the arrival of an army did not create a legitimate transfer of sovereignty; and a treaty between the invaders did not mean that Poland had accepted its disappearance. On 30 September, the Polish ambassador in Washington formally rejected the settlement made in Moscow two days earlier. The country was being divided by force while its government continued to contest the division. [1] This collection follows that process through five dates between August and October. Each marks a different kind of change: a diplomatic bargain, two successive invasions, a revised territorial agreement and the organization of German civilian rule. Read together, the dates explain how Poland lost effective control of its territory without ceasing to exist as a political cause, a recognized state or a society capable of resistance. They also distinguish what the occupiers intended from what their armies had achieved and what their administrations could enforce. The country being invaded must first be understood on its own terms. Interwar Poland extended considerably farther east than Poland does today. The Treaty of Riga of 18 March 1921 had established the Polish–Soviet frontier that remained in place until 1939. The eastern borderlands contained communities with different languages, religions and political attachments; they cannot be represented adequately as a single population awaiting one national destiny. Their diversity would become a subject of German and Soviet bargaining and propaganda, but it did not give either neighbouring government the consent of the people over whom it claimed authority. [2] [3]

23 August: bargaining over other countries

The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact changed the strategic conditions under which Germany could attack Poland. Its public provisions promised nonaggression between Germany and the Soviet Union, consultation and the avoidance of support for a third power fighting either signatory. Those promises mattered because they reduced the immediate danger that Hitler’s attack would bring Soviet opposition. Yet the published treaty was only one part of the transaction. The governments also negotiated a secret protocol dealing with territories whose inhabitants and representatives had no part in the agreement. [4] For Poland, the protocol described an approximate division of interests along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers, leaving open whether any independent Polish state would remain. Its wider provisions concerned the Baltic states, Finland and Bessarabia. This was a framework for disposing of other countries’ futures, rather than a record of territory already conquered. It neither placed Soviet soldiers inside Poland on 23 August nor established the final occupation boundary reached later in September. [5] That distinction is the starting point for the atlas. On the August date, a sphere of influence represents an understanding between governments about what they were prepared to tolerate or pursue. It is not interchangeable with military possession. The [study of the pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) examines the failed alternatives, the negotiations in Moscow and the calculations that made cooperation possible between regimes whose longer ambitions remained profoundly antagonistic.

1 September: military advantage meets resistance

Germany’s invasion turned diplomatic opportunity into an attempt to destroy the Polish armed forces. The geography favoured converging attacks: East Prussia supplied an approach from the north, German territory to the west supported the main offensive, and the southern approaches through Slovakia added another threat. Polish commanders faced a difficult choice between defending exposed industrial and population centres and withdrawing towards a shorter position that would surrender them. German strength in armour, aircraft and mobile formations made the problem more urgent, but the outcome still depended on fighting, communications, crossings and the movement of supplies. [6] The speed of the leading German formations can obscure the resistance they encountered. A column might reach a road junction while Polish troops remained active behind it; a local attack might fail while another formation advanced around the position. The Bzura counteroffensive, beginning on 9 September, demonstrates why Poland’s defeat should not be written as an uninterrupted German procession. Kutrzeba’s forces struck the flank of the German Eighth Army and forced a major response, although German concentration subsequently threatened the Polish attackers with encirclement. Tactical success and a deteriorating strategic position could exist at the same time. [7] Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September, internationalizing the conflict. Chamberlain’s announcement to Parliament explicitly connected British belligerency to Germany’s failure to promise an end to the aggression and withdrawal from Poland. A declaration, however, was different from military relief. The limited French advance in the Saar and the developing British deployment did not remove the immediate pressure on the Polish armies. Their allies were preparing for a prolonged conflict while Poland needed help within days. The [study of 1 September](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) follows that mismatch alongside the fighting and the violence inflicted on civilians. [8] [9] [10]

17 September: invasion from the east

The Red Army crossed Poland’s eastern frontier while Polish forces were still fighting Germany. Moscow presented its action as necessary protection for Ukrainians and Belarusians after an alleged collapse of the Polish state. The Soviet note reproduced in contemporary American diplomatic correspondence makes the reasoning explicit: it claimed that the disappearance of Polish government had released the Soviet Union from its treaty obligations and justified entry. That document is evidence of the excuse offered by the invading government. Its claims must be tested against the continued operation of Polish authorities, resistance in the field and recognition abroad. [11] For the people inside Poland, the second invasion transformed the meaning of the east. A direction of retreat from the German advance became another direction from which hostile forces approached. The Polish leadership crossed into Romania during the night of 17–18 September and was interned; troops sought routes towards Romania and Hungary, while other formations resisted Soviet attacks. Fighting at Grodno and elsewhere showed that the new occupation was imposed, even though the disparity of forces and the existing war against Germany sharply restricted Polish choices. [12] Foreign governments made different decisions about the new aggressor. In London on 18 September, Alexander Cadogan told American ambassador Joseph Kennedy that Britain did not consider itself automatically at war with the Soviet Union. The same report records the Polish request for a protest and British objections to the claim that Poland’s government had ceased to exist. Rejection of a justification, continued diplomatic recognition and a decision to fight were separate actions. The [study of the Soviet invasion](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) examines their consequences together with Soviet operational orders, Polish resistance and the varied experiences of soldiers and civilians. [13]

A distinction that runs through the collection

A defeated army does not sign away a state

Military surrender, occupation, annexation and international recognition concern different kinds of authority. A garrison can surrender without consenting to the partition of its country. An occupying government can impose rules without acquiring an accepted right to the territory. Poland’s formal rejection of the September settlement is central evidence of that distinction.

[1]

28 September: negotiating the division after invasion

The German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty revised the August bargain. Its public text declared the agreed boundary definitive and assigned administrative reorganization on either side to the two signatories. The accompanying secret protocol transferred Lithuania into the Soviet sphere, subject to a territorial reservation, while assigning the Lublin province and part of the Warsaw province to Germany. The later partition therefore cannot be read as the straightforward implementation of an unchanged August line. The occupiers were adjusting their arrangement as the military and political situation developed. [14] [15] Warsaw capitulated on the same date, but its surrender and the treaty were separate events. The city’s defenders were ending a siege; the governments in Moscow were asserting the authority to decide Poland’s territorial future. Polish forces continued fighting after Warsaw’s capitulation, and the final major campaign fighting at Kock ended in early October. There was no single moment at which every Polish formation surrendered, every occupation boundary became effective and every political question was settled. [16] The agreement also had an international purpose. In a joint declaration, Germany and the Soviet Union urged an end to the war between Germany and the Western powers and sought to place responsibility for its continuation on Britain and France. That argument treated the gains of conquest as an accomplished settlement before asking other governments to accept peace. The [study of 28 September](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) examines the treaty’s public and secret provisions, economic arrangements, Polish rejection and the responses in London, Paris and Washington. [17]

26 October: making occupation a system of government

The October date concerns the institutions through which Germany governed the territory it controlled. Annexed western and northern districts were incorporated into the Reich, while the General Government under Hans Frank administered another portion of occupied Poland. The latter initially comprised the districts of Kraków, Warsaw, Radom and Lublin. It was an imposed German administration, not a surviving Polish government. The distinction between annexation and the General Government reflected different territorial arrangements within the same project of domination. [18] The chronology requires care. The founding decree for the General Government bore the date 12 October, while the civilian administration took effect on 26 October. The annexation arrangements also involved separate decrees and effective dates. Such distinctions mattered because the exercise of authority developed through orders, appointments and later adjustments; it did not follow automatically from the September treaty. The [study of 26 October](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) traces those decisions into the regulation of labour, education, property and daily life. [19] Soviet occupation followed a different administrative sequence. Controlled elections in October supplied assemblies that requested incorporation into the Soviet Union, followed by formal incorporation measures on **1–2 November**. Those acts should not be dated to the invasion itself or treated as freely expressed popular consent. The German and Soviet systems differed in institutions, ideology and procedure; both used the power acquired through invasion to override Poland’s territorial independence. Their distinct chronologies are essential to understanding the different claims shown on the maps. [20]

The people inside the partition—and the Poland that continued

For civilians, the sequence was experienced through displacement, violence and changing demands. Jewish families fleeing the German advance often travelled east, only to encounter a second occupation and increasingly dangerous crossings. Some later attempted to return because separation from relatives, lack of money and uncertainty about shelter could make remaining away from home unbearable. Such decisions cannot be judged as though refugees possessed a reliable forecast of everything that would follow. The records of flight show people choosing among immediate dangers with incomplete information. [21] Nor can the population of eastern Poland be divided into uniform ethnic responses. Stanisław Boridczenko’s research on attitudes towards the armies examines the interaction of national, social and local attachments. A person’s response to arriving soldiers could depend on political hopes, previous grievances, fear, practical obligations or immediate threats. Explaining that variety neither validates Soviet claims of liberation nor erases the coercion of invasion. It prevents the occupiers’ broad categories from becoming the historian’s explanation for everyone placed within them. [3] Persecution was already acquiring an administrative form. Heydrich’s instructions of 21 September linked the concentration of Jewish populations to railway access and required Jewish councils to carry out German demands under threat. Census-taking, movement and economic decisions became instruments of coercion. This early process must be understood in its own chronology: it was part of the developing occupation, without being identical to the later, fully developed machinery of extermination. The October study follows how political and racial objectives were translated into offices, regulations and acts of dispossession. [22] Polish political life also continued beyond the occupied territory. Władysław Raczkiewicz became president and Władysław Sikorski prime minister in France on 30 September. The United States explicitly affirmed continued recognition of the Polish government on 2 October. Within occupied Poland, underground organization began to preserve a capacity for resistance. None of this restored the government’s ability to protect its population immediately. It did, however, prevent the occupiers’ description of Poland as an extinguished state from becoming an uncontested account of what had happened. [23] [24] [25]

Reading the maps and the studies together

The atlas separates events that a single end-of-campaign map would compress. Its dated views distinguish political boundaries, territorial control, administrative arrangements and military movement. An arrow indicates a direction or an explicitly identified operational objective; its tip should not automatically be read as the furthest position securely occupied on that day. A shaded area describes the kind of control identified in its legend and notes. Neither device confers legitimacy on the authority it represents. The survival of the prewar Polish outline makes it possible to compare those imposed changes against the territory over which they operated. Historical geography also involves limits of precision. Regional boundaries are generalized, and a diplomatic agreement can be better documented than the moment a particular road or village changed hands. Read the dates, explanations and source notes together rather than treating every line as a surveyed frontier. The superscript numbers in this introduction lead to identifiable sources below; each source entry links to the underlying document or study and back to its first citation. Treaty texts establish what governments agreed, while diplomatic reports establish what their authors reported or believed. Neither should silently substitute for evidence of events on the ground. The five studies can be read independently, but their sequence reveals a cumulative process: bargaining over Poland, invading it, renegotiating its division and constructing institutions to govern the conquered population. The central question remains the relationship between power and authority. Germany and the Soviet Union acquired immense power over Polish territory and its inhabitants. Poland’s continuing resistance, government and diplomatic recognition ensured that this power never amounted to a settlement accepted by the country they had divided.

summary: Five dates explain how diplomatic bargaining became invasion, partition and occupation—and why military defeat did not extinguish the Polish state.
sourceMethod: This introduction combines German–Soviet treaty texts, contemporary diplomatic correspondence, British parliamentary records, Polish documentary scholarship, military history and research on civilian experience. The main evidence includes the Institute for Western Affairs, the Polish Army Museum, the Institute of National Remembrance, The Historical Journal and the published Foreign Relations of the United States documents. Museum accounts supplement these sources. Official claims are attributed to their authors; military control, claimed annexation and diplomatic recognition are distinguished. The detailed studies supply the fuller operational and local evidence. Numbered superscripts link to sources below, and each source has a link back to its first citation.
